title: Binary Search, Invariants, and Monotonic Search Spaces
description: Master binary search: O(log n) logarithmic reduction, loop invariants, lo/hi/mid pointers, left/right boundary templates, and searching across monotone solution spaces.

sections.title: Search space halving and the O(log n) bound
sections.learning_objective: Derive logarithmic search complexity from repeated problem halving.
sections.markdown:
## When to recognize this pattern
Ordered arrays, logarithmic query limits, or monotonic boolean predicates over an answer space.

## Core idea
`Binary search` is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that finds target values in a `sorted` array in `O(log n)` time. At each step, it compares the target with the middle element `mid`. If the middle element does not match, the entire half of the array that cannot contain the target is eliminated. Halving the `search space` on every step reduces $N$ candidate elements to 1 in at most $\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ comparisons. For $N = 1,000,000,000$, binary search guarantees finding the answer in at most 30 comparisons!

examples.explanation: Executes exact-match binary search across sorted integers in O(log n) time.

key_points: Precondition: Data must be sorted or exhibit a monotonic boolean predicate property.
Calculate mid as `lo + (hi - lo) // 2` to prevent integer overflow in fixed-width languages.

sections.title: Loop invariants and left/right boundary templates
sections.learning_objective: Master robust binary search templates that eliminate off-by-one errors and infinite loops.
sections.markdown:
## Naive approach
Linear scanning checks elements sequentially in O(N) time, which times out when queries are frequent or N >= 10^6.

## Better approach
Off-by-one errors and infinite loops are the most frequent bugs in binary search. To eliminate them, maintain an unambiguous `invariant`: a mathematical truth that holds before and after each iteration. For finding boundaries (e.g. `bisect_left` / first occurrence of target or first element $\ge$ target), use the standard `template`:
- Boundary: `lo, hi = 0, len(nums)` (search space is half-open `[lo, hi)`).
- Condition: `while lo < hi:`
- Transition: If `nums[mid] < target`, target cannot be in left half, so `lo = mid + 1`. Otherwise, `hi = mid`. Upon loop termination, `lo == hi` points to the exact leftmost insertion index.

examples.explanation: Standard lower_bound template reliably finds the first valid index without infinite loops.

key_points: Half-open template [lo, hi) terminates when lo == hi, eliminating off-by-one boundary ambiguity.
Never write mid = (lo + hi) // 2 when hi can be large in compiled environments.

sections.title: Monotonicity and binary search on solution space
sections.learning_objective: Apply binary search across abstract monotonic solution spaces.
sections.markdown:
## Python implementation
Clean binary search maintains explicit half-open [lo, hi) or closed [lo, hi] pointer invariants without off-by-one errors.

## Step-by-step example
Binary search is NOT limited to searching physical arrays. It applies to any problem with a `monotone` feasibility function: a boolean predicate `is_valid(x)` that transitions from `False` to `True` (or vice-versa) at a single threshold (e.g. F, F, F, T, T, T). In 'Binary Search on Answer' (e.g. Koko Eating Bananas, Capacity to Ship Packages), we define the `search space` $[\text{lo}, \text{hi}]$ over possible candidate answers, evaluate feasibility in $O(n)$ time, and binary search for the minimum viable value in $O(n \log(\text{range}))$ time.

examples.explanation: Finds floor integer square root by binary searching over candidate integers 1..x//2.

key_points: Recognize monotonicity: if speed K works, all speeds > K also work.
Binary search on answer finds the optimal threshold in O(validation_cost * log(search_space)).

sections.title: Searching rotated and partitioned arrays
sections.learning_objective: Solve modified binary search on rotated sorted arrays.
sections.markdown:
## Time complexity
O(log N) runtime bound derived from repeatedly halving the search space.

## Space complexity
O(1) auxiliary space for iterative binary search; O(log N) stack frames for recursive implementations.

## Common mistakes
A classic interview problem is searching a `rotated` sorted array (e.g. `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`). Even when rotated, one half of the array divided at `mid` is ALWAYS normally sorted! We identify which half is sorted by comparing `nums[lo]` with `nums[mid]`:
1. If `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]`, the left half is sorted. We check if target falls within `[nums[lo], nums[mid]]`. If so, search left (`hi = mid - 1`); otherwise search right (`lo = mid + 1`).
2. If the right half is sorted, we perform the symmetric range check. This maintains the $O(\log n)$ runtime invariant.

examples.explanation: Navigates rotated sorted array by determining which sub-half preserves sorted ordering.

key_points: In a rotated sorted array, at least one half (left or right of mid) is always normally sorted.
Check whether the target lies within the boundaries of the sorted half to pick the next branch.

sections.title: Binary search interview check and Arena practice
sections.learning_objective: Transfer binary search patterns directly to Arena problems.
sections.markdown:
## Arena reference
Practice with `dsa-search-insert-position` in Forge Arena. Restate the invariant and derive your solution independently before submitting to deterministic grading.

Binary search is tested heavily in algorithmic interviews due to its strict correctness requirements.

### Common Interview Questions
1. *Why does binary search fail if `mid = (lo + hi) // 2` is used with two elements under `while lo < hi`?*
   *(When lo = 0 and hi = 1, mid = 0. If your logic sets `lo = mid`, lo remains 0, resulting in an infinite loop! Always ensure either lo advances (`lo = mid + 1`) or use upper mid `(lo + hi + 1) // 2`)*. 
2. *How do you find the first and last position of an element in a sorted array?*
   *(Run two binary searches: one lower_bound for `target`, and one lower_bound for `target + 1` minus 1)*. 
3. *When should you suspect a problem can be solved with Binary Search on Answer?*
   *(When the prompt asks for 'minimum maximum' or 'maximum minimum' and verifying a solution takes polynomial time)*. 

### Arena Practice Problems
- `dsa-search-insert-position`: Canonical lower bound index insertion
- `dsa-first-last-position`: Dual boundary binary search on duplicates
- `dsa-find-in-rotated`: Searching partitioned rotated arrays
- `dsa-sqrt-integer`: Binary search on monotone answer space

examples.code:
# First and last position via reusable lower_bound template
def search_range(nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
    left_idx = lower_bound(nums, target)
    if left_idx == len(nums) or nums[left_idx] != target:
        return [-1, -1]
    right_idx = lower_bound(nums, target + 1) - 1
    return [left_idx, right_idx]

print(search_range([5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], 8))
print(search_range([5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], 6))
examples.explanation: Executes dual binary searches to identify target boundaries in O(log n) time.

key_points: Practice boundary templates until you can write them without looking at references.
Always check edge cases: empty array, 1-element array, target smaller than nums[0], target larger than nums[-1].

summary: Binary search reduces candidate elements by half at each step, delivering O(log n) runtime.
Preconditions require sorted data or a monotonic boolean feasibility function.
Loop invariants prevent infinite loops: specify whether interval is closed [lo, hi] or half-open [lo, hi).
Binary Search on Answer finds optimal thresholds across abstract monotonic solution spaces.
Rotated sorted arrays maintain at least one sorted half, preserving logarithmic lookup efficiency.
interview_takeaways: State your search space interval [lo, hi] and loop invariant explicitly to the interviewer before coding.
Use `mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2` to demonstrate software engineering rigor regarding integer overflow.
When you hear 'find the minimum capacity' or 'find the maximum allocation', immediately think Binary Search on Answer.
common_mistakes: Using `lo = mid` in a `while lo < hi` loop without upper-mid bias, creating an infinite loop on 2-element arrays
Assuming binary search only works on static arrays, missing Binary Search on Answer opportunities
Calculating `mid = (lo + hi) // 2` in languages with 32-bit signed integers where lo + hi overflows
Forgetting to check if the found index matches the target before returning in boundary searches
